meta.title_plain: How six LEGO bricks hide 915 million builds
meta.teaser: Six small bricks, 915 million builds, and a famous number that was wrong.

page.title: How six LEGO bricks hide 915 million builds
page.sub: The story of the maths inside six LEGO bricks
page.bigIdea: Six classic 2×4 bricks can be put together in 915,103,765 different ways. It took a maths professor and a computer to count them all.

cards.title: Start with just two bricks
cards.front: How many ways can two 2×4 bricks click together?
cards.back: There are 46 spots to click one brick onto another. Spin the pair around and many builds look the same. That leaves 24 truly different builds.
cards.tryit: Grab two 2×4 bricks. In 10 minutes, how many different ways can you join them? Aim for 10.

cards.title: Every brick multiplies the options
cards.front: Add a third brick and the number explodes.
cards.back: Each new brick on top has 46 spots again. So a tower multiplies by 46 each time. Six bricks in a tower give about 103 million builds.
cards.tryit: Build a three-brick tower. Now slide only the top brick one stud at a time. How many new towers can you make?

cards.title: The famous number was wrong
cards.front: For years, people believed six bricks made 102,981,500 builds.
cards.back: That 1974 LEGO number only counted towers six bricks tall. It left out lower, wider builds. It was even off by four, probably due to a small calculator.
cards.tryit: Use six bricks to make a build only two bricks tall. That's a build the old count missed!

cards.title: A computer counts it all
cards.front: In 2004, maths professor Søren Eilers wrote a program to count every build.
cards.back: It ran for about half a week on a home computer. The answer: 915,103,765. A high school student, Mikkel Abrahamsen, wrote his own program and got the same number.
cards.tryit: Write a tiny 'program' on paper: steps to list every two-brick build without missing or repeating one.

cards.title: In-between height wins
cards.front: Which six-brick builds are most common: tall, low or in between?
cards.back: Builds four bricks tall win, with about 360 million. Only about 8 million are two bricks tall. And seven bricks? About 86 billion builds!
cards.tryit: Build a six-brick model exactly four bricks tall. Can you make it look like a robot, a ship or a car?

words.d: One possible way to arrange or put things together.
The small round bump on top of a LEGO brick.
When something looks the same after you turn or flip it.
Add a number to itself many times, like 46 × 46.
Step-by-step instructions a computer follows to do a job.

quiz.q: Each new brick on a tower has 46 spots. How many ways can you stack 3 bricks, before removing look-alikes?
quiz.hint: Two bricks get placed on the bottom one, and each has 46 choices. Add or multiply?
quiz.why: Each placed brick has 46 choices, so 46 × 46 = 2,116 towers.

quiz.q: Two bricks have 46 click spots but only 24 different builds. Why fewer?
opts: Some spots make the bricks fall off
Spinning a build makes two spots look the same
quiz.hint: Build one, then spin it halfway around on the table.
quiz.why: Most builds match another one when spun, so 44 pair up into 22, plus 2 that match themselves.

quiz.q: 915 million is about how many times bigger than 103 million?
quiz.why: 915 ÷ 103 is close to 9, so the real count is almost nine times bigger.

quiz.q: Why was the old 1974 number so much smaller?
opts: It only counted towers six bricks tall
quiz.hint: Think about the low build you made for card 3.
quiz.why: It skipped all the lower, wider builds, and those turned out to be most of them.

page.think: If you counted one build every second without stopping, how long would 915 million take? What other huge numbers might hide in Roblox, Brawl Stars or your own LEGO box?
